prompt: A test fails to reject the null hypothesis that a new routing system changes nothing. What can Horta conclude?
hint: A trial's verdict is 'not guilty', never 'innocent'.

choices.text: That the new system has no effect
choices.why: Not rejecting is 'not guilty', not 'innocent': the data was not strong enough, which is different.

choices.text: That the data did not show an effect
choices.why: Right. An effect might be real and too small for this sample to detect.

choices.text: That the new system makes deliveries slower
choices.why: Nothing in a non-rejection points the other way.

choices.text: That the test was run wrongly
choices.why: A non-rejection is an ordinary result of a correct test.

prompt: Put the four steps of a hypothesis test in order.
hint: The level is chosen before the data is used.
items: State the null and alternative hypotheses
Compute the test statistic from the sample
trap: Choosing the significance level after computing the statistic lets the data pick its own threshold.

prompt: Why does a test assume the null hypothesis rather than the alternative?
hint: Which one names a single value?

choices.text: The null is more likely to be true
choices.why: The test takes no view on which is more likely.

choices.text: The alternative cannot be tested at all
choices.why: The alternative is what a rejection supports; the issue is that it makes no single prediction.

choices.text: It makes one precise prediction to check
choices.why: Right. 'μ = 40' predicts a specific distribution for the statistic; 'μ < 40' does not.

choices.text: Because statisticians are pessimists
choices.why: It is about having something precise to compare the data with.

prompt: Which is a correctly written null hypothesis for 'is the machine on its 1000 g target?'

choices.why: Hypotheses are about the population mean μ; the sample mean is already known.
Right. The null names one precise value of the population mean.
That is the two-sided alternative.
A null holds the equals sign; this is a one-sided alternative.

prompt: Match each question to its alternative hypothesis.
hint: The alternative is what you hope or fear to find.

pairs.left: Did the new routing make deliveries faster than 40 minutes?
Is the machine off its 1000 g target?
Does the new page convert more than the old one?

prompt: An analyst sees the sample mean fell, then runs a one-sided test for 'fell'. What is wrong?

choices.text: The direction was chosen after seeing the data
choices.why: Right. That halves the threshold in the data's favour and makes a 5% test behave like a 10% one.

choices.text: One-sided tests are never allowed
choices.why: They are allowed when the direction comes from the question, before the data.

choices.text: The test should have been on the sample mean
choices.why: Tests are always about the population.

choices.text: A fall needs a larger significance level
choices.why: The level does not depend on the direction of the change.

prompt: With α = 0.05 and 24 degrees of freedom, why is the two-sided threshold (±2.06) further out than the one-sided one (−1.71)?
hint: Where does each test put its 5%?

choices.text: Two-sided tests use more data
choices.why: Same data; only the split of α differs.

choices.text: Each tail holds only 2.5%
choices.why: Right. Splitting the 5% between two tails pushes each threshold further out.

choices.text: Two-sided tests use a different distribution
choices.why: Both use the same t distribution with 24 degrees of freedom.

choices.text: The one-sided test is less accurate
choices.why: It is not less accurate; it looks in one direction only.

prompt: A sample of 16 has mean 52 and standard deviation 8. What is t against a null of 50?
Two samples both have a mean 3 minutes below the null's 40. Which gives the larger t?

choices.text: The one with the larger standard deviation
choices.why: More noise means a larger standard error and a smaller t.

choices.text: Both give the same t, since the difference is the same
choices.why: The same signal over different noise gives different t.

choices.text: The smaller sample, as each value counts more
choices.why: A smaller sample has a larger standard error, so a smaller t.

choices.text: The larger, less noisy one
choices.why: Right. A larger n and a smaller s both shrink the standard error, raising the signal-to-noise ratio.

prompt: The t statistic divides the difference from the null by the standard ___.
If the null hypothesis is true and α = 0.05, how often will a test reject it?

choices.text: Never
choices.why: Even a true null produces extreme samples by chance.

choices.text: 5% of the time
choices.why: Right. α is the false-alarm rate on true nulls.

choices.text: 95% of the time
choices.why: That is how often a true null is kept.

choices.text: It depends on the sample size
choices.why: For a true null the rejection rate is α at any sample size.

prompt: Horta runs 40 independent tests, each at α = 0.05, on changes that in fact do nothing. About how many will come out significant?
Why must α be chosen before the data is seen?
hint: What would choosing it afterwards let somebody do?

choices.text: Because spreadsheets need it as an input
choices.why: Software convenience is not the reason.

choices.text: Because α changes once the data is collected
choices.why: α changes only if somebody changes it, which is the danger.

choices.text: Otherwise it controls nothing
choices.why: Right. A level picked to fit the result makes the false-alarm rate whatever the data needed.

choices.text: Because the critical value can only be read from a table in advance
choices.why: Critical values can be read any time; the timing matters for honesty, not for arithmetic.

prompt: For the 25 routing deliveries, mean 38.9 and standard error 1.10, what is t against the null of 40? Give two decimal places.
Fifteen bags average 1004.6 g, t = 4.21, and the null μ = 1000 is rejected. What does the test add that the 95% interval of 1002.3 to 1006.9 g did not already say?

choices.text: How far off target the machine is
choices.why: That is the interval's contribution, not the test's.

choices.text: That the machine is accurate to the gram
choices.why: Nothing here says that; the machine is several grams over.

choices.text: Little: 1000 lies outside the interval anyway
choices.why: Right. A 95% interval that excludes 1000 and a two-sided 5% test that rejects 1000 say the same thing; the interval also says how far.

choices.text: That the result will repeat with the next 15 bags
choices.why: No single test guarantees that.

prompt: After a non-significant result on 25 deliveries, the supplier says: 'So the system works no worse than before.' What is the flaw?
hint: What question was the test built to answer?

choices.text: There is no flaw; not rejecting proves no change
choices.why: Not rejecting proves nothing of the kind; it means the evidence was weak.

choices.text: The test was never designed to show 'no worse'
choices.why: Right. It asked whether deliveries were faster; a non-rejection cannot be turned into a claim of equivalence.

choices.text: 25 deliveries is too many for a t test
choices.why: There is no upper limit; 25 is on the small side.

choices.text: The significance level should have been 0.5
choices.why: A level of 0.5 would reject half of all true nulls.
